passage: In the green room behind the school auditorium, ten minutes before the inter-school debate, Tushar's stomach churned like a washing machine. "I'm going to be sick. I can't go on," he told Ms Seema, the debate coach. She didn't argue. "Let's slow down. When did you last eat?" He thought. He'd skipped lunch to practise. "And what else is your body doing?" "Hands cold. Heart fast. But... I also keep grinning." "So some of it might be hunger, and some might be excitement, not only fear." She handed him a banana from her bag. He ate it, breathed out slowly twice, and noticed the churn had shrunk to a flutter. When his name was called, the flutter felt almost like a drumroll.

qa.q: Why had Tushar skipped lunch?
qa.a: He had skipped lunch to practise.

qa.q: What did Tushar first think his churning stomach meant, and what else was going on?
qa.a: He thought he was too scared to go on, but he was also hungry and a bit excited.

qa.q: How did Ms Seema help Tushar read his body better?
qa.a: She slowed him down, asked about food and other signals, and helped him see the whole pattern before deciding it was fear.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ms Seema had simply told Tushar not to be nervous?
qa.a: He might have stayed hungry and convinced he was only afraid, and perhaps pulled out of the debate.

grounding: Shows a teenager misreading a churning stomach as pure fear, and slowing down to notice the whole pattern of hunger, nerves and excitement.

passage:
"You've had that headache since Monday," Santosh said, switching on the light. "It's two a.m."
"It's nothing. Weak people stop. The project's due Friday." Ramesh rubbed his neck without looking up.
"You fell asleep standing in the mess queue."
"I was resting my eyes."
"Your jaw's been clenched all week. You snapped at the lab assistant."
"Because he's slow."
"Because you haven't slept. Remember Kiran last semester? Pushed through, then fainted in the viva and had to repeat the year."
Ramesh was quiet. His temples throbbed.
"Sleep now. I'll wake you at seven. If the headache's still there tomorrow, we go to the health centre."
"...Seven. Not a minute later."
"Fine. Lights off."

qa.q: Where did Ramesh fall asleep standing?
qa.a: In the mess queue.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's "Weak people stop" reveal about how he sees his tiredness?
qa.a: He feels ashamed of being tired, treating discomfort as weakness, and is driven by pressure about the Friday deadline.

qa.q: What sensible steps does Santosh push for?
qa.a: Sleeping now with a seven o'clock wake-up, and going to the health centre if the headache is still there tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Ramesh's week?
qa.a: Santosh sees a pattern of warning signs, the headache, clenched jaw, dozing and snapping, heading toward a collapse like Kiran's.

grounding: Shows a young adult pushing through headache, tension and exhaustion for a project, mistaking discomfort for weakness, and a friend urging him to listen before he collapses.

passage: The lunch rush at the roadside dhaba outside Moga had lasted three hours, and Baljeet felt a snap rising when Lakshmi asked, for the second time, where the extra ghee tin was. Instead of answering, Baljeet did what had become a habit since winter: stepped behind the tandoor, closed both eyes for a minute and checked. Jaw clenched. Shoulders up. Stomach hollow. Breath short and high. "You haven't eaten since six," Baljeet muttered, "and you're tired, not angry at her." A plate of dal and two rotis, eaten standing, and a slow breath out. Then back to the counter. "Ghee's under the bench, left side. Sorry, I was about to bite your head off." Lakshmi laughed. "I saw. Go on, eat another roti."

qa.q: Where is the extra ghee tin?
qa.a: Under the bench, on the left side.

qa.q: What was Baljeet really feeling when the snap rose, and how did the check show it?
qa.a: The clenched jaw, raised shoulders, hollow stomach and short breath showed Baljeet was hungry and tired, not truly angry at Lakshmi.

qa.q: Why is this one-minute check a useful habit?
qa.a: It catches hunger, stress and fatigue before they turn into snapping, so Baljeet can eat, breathe and answer kindly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt if Baljeet had snapped instead?
qa.a: Lakshmi would likely have felt hurt or annoyed over a simple question, and the rush would have felt even harder.

grounding: Shows a person pausing for a minute to notice jaw, shoulders, stomach and breathing, and catching hunger and fatigue before they turn into snapping.

subtype: People who feel body signals differently [Observer]
passage: For months I thought my colleague Abhinav was just careless about lunch. I'm Zeenat, and I sat opposite him in the design team. He'd work straight through till four, then suddenly go pale and shaky, and once he snapped at the intern over a font. I'll admit I rolled my eyes and said, "Just eat when you're hungry, na?" He looked at me, tired. "I don't really feel hungry until it's too late. My body's signals come in very quiet. I'm neurodivergent, and it's common for people like me." I felt awful. After that he set a phone reminder for one o'clock, and I started knocking on his desk when I went for lunch. No lecture, just "Coming?" Most days he comes. The four o'clock crashes have nearly stopped.

qa.q: What time did Abhinav set a phone reminder for?
qa.a: For one o'clock.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel after Abhinav explained, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat felt awful and a bit ashamed for rolling eyes and blaming him for a signal he couldn't easily feel.

qa.q: What support works for Abhinav without blaming him?
qa.a: A phone reminder at one o'clock and a friendly knock on the desk for lunch, with no lecture.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt when Zeenat said "Just eat when you're hungry"?
qa.a: He likely felt tired and misunderstood, blamed for missing a signal his body sends only faintly.

grounding: Shows a colleague learning that a neurodivergent coworker feels hunger faintly, and respecting this with reminders and routine instead of blame.

subtype: Headaches and stomach aches from school worry [Actor]
passage: Every Monday morning in their Toronto apartment, Yuki's stomach hurt. It was real: she curled up on the couch, pale, and couldn't finish her toast. By Saturday it was always gone. Her father, Omar, took her to the family doctor, who pressed her tummy, asked questions and found nothing wrong in her body. "The pain is real," the doctor said. "Sometimes worries show up in the stomach." That evening Omar sat on her bed. "Is something at school heavy right now?" Yuki picked at the blanket. Then it came out: a spelling test every Monday, read aloud, and two girls who laughed whenever she stumbled. Omar listened, told her it wasn't her fault, and emailed her teacher that same night. The next Monday, Yuki's stomach hurt a little less.

qa.q: What happens at school every Monday?
qa.a: A spelling test, read aloud.

qa.q: What was Yuki worried about that showed up as stomach pain?
qa.a: She was anxious and embarrassed about the Monday spelling test and the two girls who laughed when she stumbled.

qa.q: Which steps did Omar take, and why were they sensible?
qa.a: He had the doctor check first, then gently asked about school, listened, and emailed the teacher that same night.

qa.q: How might the doctor see Yuki's stomach aches?
qa.a: The doctor treats the pain as real while suspecting worry behind it, so it deserves attention rather than dismissal.

grounding: Shows a child under school pressure developing real stomach pain with no physical cause, and adults treating it as genuine while attending to the emotional load.

subtype: Tired, tense and unwell in exam season [Actor]
passage: Last March, during my Class 12 boards, my body felt like it belonged to someone much older. I'm Lalremsiami, and for three weeks I had a headache from morning to night, a stomach that turned at the smell of rice, and shoulders so tight I couldn't turn my head to check the clock. I was tired all the time but lay awake doing sums in the dark. I thought I was falling apart. My tuition teacher, Hemant sir, noticed me rubbing my neck and asked me to stay back. He didn't lecture. He said exam stress lives in the body too, and asked what I'd eaten and how I'd slept. He made me promise three things: a proper meal, a walk round the Aizawl lanes before revision, and lights out by eleven. And if the headaches kept on, a doctor. They eased by the second week. I still did the sums, just in daylight.

qa.q: What three things did Hemant sir ask Lalremsiami to promise?
qa.a: A proper meal, a walk round the Aizawl lanes before revision, and lights out by eleven.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel about all these symptoms at the time?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt scared and overwhelmed, thinking everything was falling apart.

qa.q: Why was Hemant sir's approach helpful?
qa.a: He explained that stress shows up in the body, gave simple steps for food, movement and sleep, and pointed to a doctor if the headaches continued.

qa.q: What might Hemant sir have noticed that made him ask Lalremsiami to stay back?
qa.a: He noticed the neck-rubbing and probably a tired, tense student, and felt concerned enough to check in.

grounding: Shows a teenager in exam season with headaches, an upset stomach, tight muscles and constant tiredness, eased by rest, food, movement and a trusted adult's reassurance.

passage:
"Mummy, my stomach hurts again."
"Again? Every day before school, Disha. It's drama." Indu kept rolling the rotis.
"It's not drama. It really hurts."
"Last week it was your head. Next it'll be your toe."
Disha went to her room and shut the door softly. That evening she didn't come for dinner.
Indu knocked. "Disha? Aren't you eating?"
"Why? You'll just say I'm faking."
Silence. Then Indu came in and sat on the bed. "I said drama because I was scared it was something else, and I was tired. That wasn't fair." She paused. "Tomorrow we'll see Dr Kamath. Both things: we check your stomach, and you tell me what's happening at school."
Disha's eyes filled. "The maths sir shouts at me every day."
Indu took her hand. "Then tell me now. I'm listening."

qa.q: Which doctor does Indu say they will see?
qa.a: Dr Kamath.

qa.q: Why did Disha skip dinner?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unheard after being called dramatic, and expected to be told she was faking.

qa.q: What did Indu change that opened the way to talking?
qa.a: She admitted that dismissing the pain wasn't fair, promised a medical check, and asked about school, which let Disha share the real worry.

qa.q: Why might Indu have reacted with "It's drama" at first?
qa.a: She admits she was scared it was something else and was tired, so brushing it off felt easier than worrying.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose pain is dismissed as drama feeling unheard, and a parent who takes it seriously, plans a medical check and opens the way to talk about stress.

passage: Three weeks before the state recruitment exam, Jaya woke in her room above the family's sweet shop in Barabanki with her heart racing so fast she thought something was bursting. Her jaw ached from clenching, her neck felt like wire, and her stomach had been bad for days. She lay rigid, sure it was her heart. In the morning her friend Asif, who worked at the chemist's down the lane, walked her to the government clinic. The doctor listened to her chest, ran a heart test and said her heart looked healthy. "Your body is carrying a lot of pressure. That can feel very frightening." Walking back past the bangle stalls, Jaya felt her shoulders drop. She still had the exam. But now, when her heart raced at night, she knew what it was, and breathed out slowly until it eased.

qa.q: What did the doctor say about Jaya's heart?
qa.a: The doctor said her heart looked healthy.

qa.q: What was Jaya afraid of when she woke with a racing heart?
qa.a: She was terrified that something was wrong with her heart, that something was bursting.

qa.q: Why did the clinic visit help, even though the exam pressure stayed?
qa.a: It ruled out other causes, and seeing the symptoms as stress lowered her fear, so she could calm her body at night.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt walking Jaya to the clinic?
qa.a: Asif was probably worried for Jaya but steady, glad to help her get checked instead of lying awake afraid.

grounding: Shows a young adult under heavy exam pressure with a racing heart, clenched jaw and bad stomach, where a medical check and seeing stress as a body event lower her fear.

passage: Bidisha, you remind me of myself at twenty-five, so let your old boss Rajni tell you a story. I was in audit then, and I said yes to everything. For two years I caught every cold that went round the office, my back ached as if I'd carried bricks, and I slept ten hours on Sundays and still woke up tired. Worse, I stopped caring. Files I used to love felt like grey sand. Everyone said, "Take a holiday." So I went to Goa for a week, came back, and by Wednesday I was exactly where I'd started. The turning point was a doctor who asked, "What will change in your work when you go back?" Nothing, I said. So I went to my manager and gave up two clients. That's when my body started to recover. So, Bidisha. What will change in yours?

qa.q: Where did Rajni go on holiday?
qa.a: To Goa, for a week.

qa.q: How did young Rajni feel about the audit files after two years of overload?
qa.a: Rajni felt detached and drained; files Rajni used to love felt like grey sand.

qa.q: What turning point in the story led to real recovery?
qa.a: The doctor's question made Rajni see nothing would change, so Rajni asked the manager to cut the load by two clients.

qa.q: How might Rajni's manager have seen the request to give up two clients?
qa.a: The manager may have been surprised, but the request gave an honest picture of an overloaded employee.

grounding: Illustrates a worker in long-term overload with constant tiredness, frequent colds, aches and detachment, whose body needed a change in workload rather than only a holiday.

subtype: Reading the body as a signal and acting [Response]
passage:
I share a cubicle wall with Ramesh at the insurance office, so I noticed things before he said anything. By September he was rubbing his temples every afternoon, chewing antacids like sweets, and grinding his teeth so hard on calls that I could hear it. I don't know what was going on in his head. But in October something changed. He took a Thursday morning off and came back saying the doctor had found nothing serious but had asked a lot about his workload. The next week he told our manager he couldn't lead two projects at once, and handed one to Suresh. He started leaving at six, and on Sunday I saw him walking in the park with his brother. The temple-rubbing hasn't stopped completely. But I don't hear the teeth anymore.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Ramesh hand to Suresh?
qa.a: One of the two projects he had been leading.

qa.q: What might Ramesh have been feeling by September, judging by the signs Lakshmi saw?
qa.a: He was probably stressed and tense, rubbing his temples, grinding his teeth and chewing antacids, though Lakshmi couldn't know for sure.

qa.q: Which of Ramesh's steps show him reading his body's signals wisely?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor, cutting his load by handing over a project, leaving at six and walking on Sundays.

qa.q: How has the change affected Lakshmi, who shares the cubicle wall?
qa.a: Lakshmi no longer hears the grinding teeth and seems relieved to see Ramesh steadier.

grounding: Shows a person who notices repeated stress symptoms seeing a doctor, reducing his load, talking to someone and rebuilding rest routines.
